M1-DATA.text: Read injury and belt-use data (NHES 3) to compare rates and explain that injury is predictable, not random.

M1-MECH.text: Explain how seat belts and helmets reduce injury by spreading force and lengthening stopping time (NHES 1).

M1-MYTH.text: Correct common seat belt myths with accurate facts (NHES 1).

M2-RECOG.text: Tell cardiac arrest from a heart attack and recognize the signs of cardiac arrest (NHES 1).

M2-CHAIN.text: Put the Chain of Survival links in order (NHES 1).

M2-TECH.text: Read compression rate from a trace and judge technique (NHES 7).

M2-SCOPE.text: Choose hands-only CPR or CPR with breaths for the situation, and know the C-A-B order (NHES 1, 7).

M2-AED.text: Put the steps of AED use in order (NHES 7).

M3-MYTH.text: Match common organ-donation myths with accurate facts (NHES 8).

M3-MSG.text: Choose an accurate, respectful message that corrects a myth (NHES 8).

M3-CHECK.text: Judge which statements about donation are myths (NHES 8, 3).

M4-PLAN.text: Plan a home fire escape: alarms, two ways out and an outside meeting spot (NHES 7).

M4-FIRE.text: Respond to a fire: get low, close doors, never go back, and know the extinguisher classes and when to fight a fire (NHES 7).

M4-AID.text: Decide between treating a minor cut or burn yourself and getting help (NHES 7).

chapters.title: Predictable, Not Random
chapters.intro: Injuries follow patterns, and patterns can be studied. Run the crash lab, explore the belt-use data, then show what you learned.

stimulus.title: Crash lab
stimulus.lead: Crash the dummy, test the helmet, drop the egg, and open the belt-use data. Change one thing at a time and watch what changes.

chips.label: Bike crash with and without a helmet
Egg test with and without the sheet

stimulus.title: Unintentional injury death rates, ages 15 to 19, United States, 2024
stimulus.alt: Bar chart of death rates per 100,000 people ages 15 to 19 in 2024. Motor vehicle traffic 12.0. Poisoning 3.8. Drowning 1.0.

items.prompt: Which statement does the chart support?

options.text: Drowning ranked second among these three causes for this age group.
Drowning deaths happened at nearly the same rate as poisoning deaths.
Poisoning deaths happened at about twice the motor vehicle traffic rate.
Motor vehicle traffic deaths happened at about six times the drowning rate.
Motor vehicle traffic deaths happened at about three times the poisoning rate.

stimulus.title: Front-seat belt use, United States, 2025
stimulus.note: Figures as shown in the Day 1 slides and handout. NHTSA reports 91.3% for all front-seat occupants in 2025.
head: Group
Belt use

items.prompt: Imagine 1,000 drivers aged 16 to 24. If their belt use matched the national rate in the table, how many MORE of them would buckle up?

stimulus.text: A class models a crash with a toy cart, an egg and a stretched sheet. The egg rides in the sheet on the cart, and the cart is pushed toward a solid block.
Model sensors are not shown here. Use the picture and what you know about crashes.

items.prompt: Match each part of the model to what it stands for in a real car crash. One choice is not used.

cards.text: The seat belt
The car itself
The solid object the car hits
The person riding in the car
The airbag

stimulus.text: These are things people say about seat belts. Match each belief to the fact that answers it.

items.prompt: Match each belief to the fact that answers it. Two facts are not used.

cards.text: Nearly every teen already buckles up on every trip, so reminders add little value.
Belts only help when a vehicle is going faster than highway speed in a crash.
Crash forces do not depend on who is riding, and male youth die from unintentional injuries at higher rates.
For front-seat riders, belts cut fatal-injury risk by about 60% in SUVs, trucks and vans.
Airbags are built to work together with seat belts, not to replace them.
Other drivers can cause a crash, and a belt protects you from mistakes your own skill cannot control.

targets.label: “My vehicle is big, so a belt is not needed.”
“Boys are tough enough to ride without a belt.”
“I’m a careful driver, so I don’t need a belt.”

chapters.title: Chain of Survival
chapters.intro: Seconds matter when a heart stops. Practice a calm, correct response in three different emergencies and with an AED, then show what you know.

stimulus.title: Rescue practice
stimulus.lead: Handle three emergencies and one AED. You choose what to do and in what order. The scene reacts to what you do.

stimulus.text: Two different heart emergencies can look alike from far away. An emergency card at a school nurse’s office lists six descriptions.

items.prompt: Sort each description under the problem it best describes.

cards.text: The heart’s electrical signal goes wrong and the heart stops pumping blood.
The person suddenly collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally.
A blocked artery cuts blood flow to part of the heart muscle.
The person is awake and says the chest feels tight or heavy.
Rescuers need to start CPR and use an AED without waiting.
Symptoms may build slowly while the person is still talking.

stimulus.text: A first-aid poster shows the Chain of Survival, five links that save lives when they are done in the right order.

items.prompt: Put the five links of the Chain of Survival in order, from the first link to the last.

steps.text: Call 911 so help is on the way
Recognize that the person is in cardiac arrest
Hand the person over to EMS when they arrive
Use an AED as soon as one arrives

stimulus.text: A coach timed a bystander giving compressions to a training manikin for 10 seconds.

items.prompt: Each bar is one compression. What was the compression rate, in compressions per minute?

items.topic: Hands-only CPR or CPR with breaths
items.prompt: Which plan fits this situation best?
scene: A lifeguard pulls a 3-year-old girl out of the pool. She does not respond and is not breathing. Another lifeguard calls 911 and sends someone for the AED. You are the next trained person to help.

options.text: Wait for the AED to arrive before touching her so nothing is done out of order.
Give only rescue breaths and check her pulse every minute until EMS takes over.
Press on her belly to push the water out, then start compressions.
Give CPR with rescue breaths and compressions, because her breathing stopped first.
Give hands-only compressions at a steady pace and skip the breaths, as for a sudden adult collapse.

stimulus.text: A teen collapsed at a track meet. A bystander has been giving compressions, and a coach just brought the school’s AED.

items.prompt: Put these actions in the order you would do them once the AED is at the person’s side.

steps.text: Turn on the AED and follow its voice prompts
Attach the pads to the bare chest as pictured
Restart chest compressions right away when the AED says to
Stand clear and press the shock button only if the AED advises it
Make sure no one touches the person while the AED analyzes

chapters.title: Myth vs. Fact: Organ Donation
chapters.intro: People share claims about organ donation all the time, and some are wrong. Practice checking claims in a fictional social feed, then show you can correct a myth accurately and respectfully.

stimulus.title: Check the feed
stimulus.lead: Read the posts in a fictional app, tag each one, and see what the facts say. Then walk through a practice registry screen.

stimulus.text: Teacher note: this is information, not a request to register. Registration decisions belong to families.

items.prompt: Match each myth to the fact that corrects it. Two facts are not used.

cards.text: A donor’s family has to pay the hospital for the donation, which is why many people skip it.
Registered donors are matched to the first patient who asks, so the decision comes down to timing.
Your doctors work to save your life first, and donation is only considered after death is declared.
Age and health conditions do not automatically rule you out; the transplant team decides what can be used.
The body is treated with care and dressed for the service, so donation does not show at an open casket.

targets.label: “I’m too old, or I have a health condition, so I can’t be a donor.”
“Donating organs means I can’t have an open-casket funeral.”
“Doctors won’t try as hard to save me if I’m a registered donor.”

items.prompt: Which reply corrects the myth best?
scene: A classmate posts on the class group chat: “No way I’m signing up as a donor. Then I couldn’t even have an open casket.” You decide to reply.

options.text: That’s false, and honestly it’s a pretty selfish way to think. You should register today so you can help people.
That’s true for organs, but if someone donates only their eyes they can still have an open casket at the funeral.
Funeral homes can fix almost anything, so it never really matters. Everyone should just register, no questions asked.
Don’t worry about it. Registered donors always get to choose exactly how their funeral is done, whatever the family wants.
Donation doesn’t rule that out. The body is dressed for the service, so it isn’t visible. It’s your family’s call, but those are the facts.

stimulus.text: Fictional statements for practice. Each could appear in a social post.

items.prompt: Select every statement that is a myth.

options.text: More than 100,000 people in the U.S. are waiting for an organ transplant.
Corneas and heart valves cannot be donated, only whole organs like hearts.
A transplant patient can be matched with a donor who is not a relative.
Celebrities are moved to the top of the transplant list because of their fame.
Blood type is one of the medical factors used to match an organ.
A donor’s family has to pay the surgeon’s fee for removing the organs.

chapters.title: Home and School Safety
chapters.intro: You may have only a minute or two to get out of a burning building, and a few simple steps make a big difference. Build an escape plan, run two fires, and treat some injuries, then show what you learned.

stimulus.title: Home safety practice
stimulus.lead: Build an escape plan, run two fires with your plan, and treat four injuries at the first-aid bench.

chips.label: Get out safely in both fire runs

stimulus.text: A different family is planning its fire escape. Use the plan of their house.

items.prompt: Match each numbered spot on the plan to what it is. One choice is not used.

cards.text: A smoke alarm outside the sleeping rooms
The outside meeting spot
A smoke alarm inside a bedroom
The second way out of a bedroom
The best place to hide from smoke

scene: You are sleeping over at a friend’s house, in a basement room with a door and one small window high on the wall. The smoke alarm goes off in the night. You smell smoke and see a gray haze near the ceiling.

options.text: Stand up and gather your phone, shoes and bag so you have everything outside.
Hide under the bed until the fire department arrives to find you in the room.
Open each door on the way to check where the fire started before you decide.
Stay low under the smoke, head for the nearest clear way out and close doors behind you.
Go back in for your friend’s dog as soon as you are safely outside the house.

stimulus.text: A school hallway has fire extinguishers on the wall. Each is marked with a class letter that says what kind of fire it is made for.

items.prompt: Match each extinguisher class to the kind of fire it is made for. Two choices are not used.

cards.text: Any fire, even one spreading across the room
A fire that is blocking the only way out
Burning wood, paper, cloth or trash
Burning liquids such as gasoline, oil or paint
Live electrical equipment that is plugged in

stimulus.text: A school nurse sorts injuries into the ones students can treat themselves and the ones that need a professional.

items.prompt: Sort each injury into the group where it belongs.

cards.text: A deep cut across the palm that gapes open
Bleeding still going after 15 minutes of pressing with a clean cloth
A burn on the hand from a chemical spill
A scrape from a bike fall with no signs of infection
A burn on the face from hot steam
A paper cut that stops bleeding with light pressure
A burn on the forearm, smaller than your palm, from a curling iron
